reason: A false success signal in one area (migrations) that a run actually fell into and that no check, policy, doc page or task-wide rule owns, so it goes in .agents/memory/migrations.md with the follow-up step of running `make db-status`.

The release freeze is a team decision that people shipping releases need as much as agents do, and the pull-request check and command policy can't reliably block a release, so a page in docs/ should own it and memory should link to it.

This is a command that looks right but isn't: it really happened (an untested migration was reported as tested), a fresh session would repeat it, nothing else in the repository owns it, and no policy rule can enforce it, so it goes in the migrations memory file until the Makefile target is fixed to fail when the database is down.

The policy matches shell commands by their leading words, so it can allow `make db-migrate ENV=test` and deny or ask for a bare `make db-migrate`; the team's table puts what a policy can enforce ahead of memory.

The release freeze is a team decision that people need as well as agents, so a page in docs/ should own it (memory can link to it); a date-based check is more than this change can add, and not every task needs it in AGENTS.md.

The command reports success when it has done nothing, so a written warning can be missed; a check, for example a database-connectivity check in the migrate target or a hook, should make `make db-migrate` exit non-zero when the database is down.

This is a trap in the migrations area: `make db-migrate` looks safe for local work but hits the shared dev database because of an `ENV=dev` default 200 lines away, which a run reading the target won't see; and since the policy matches leading words, it can't tell the safe and unsafe forms apart, so it belongs in `.agents/memory/` (e.g. migrations.md).

Running `make db-migrate` without `ENV=test` changes the development database the whole team shares, so the permission policy should enforce it for every harness (ask or deny plain `make db-migrate`, allow `make db-migrate ENV=test`) instead of relying on agents remembering a note.

The release freeze from December 15 to January 5 is a lasting team policy that people and agents look up when planning releases, so it belongs on a release-process page in docs/ rather than in instructions every run reads.
The Makefile already defines the default and its effect, so the first matching row says to point readers to that file rather than duplicate the fact.
A check can require database connectivity and verify that migrations actually applied, preventing a successful exit code from being mistaken for a completed test.
The release freeze is a team standard that people changing and releasing code need to know, so a documentation page owns it.
This is an observed trap in migration tooling: the command reports success without applying migrations, misleading later runs into treating untested work as tested.
The permission policy can require the leading words `make db-migrate ENV=test` and reject the bare command, preventing local migrations from targeting the shared development database.
A team release-freeze schedule is neither a product fact nor a repository trap; ask where the team keeps its release calendar.
Add a check that fails when the database is unavailable and verifies migrations actually ran, so a zero exit status cannot falsely count as successful testing.
The release freeze is a shared team scheduling policy that belongs in release documentation in docs/.
Enforce ENV=test for local migrations with a command guard or shared permission policy so omitting it cannot modify the team’s shared development database.
